description: We are USTACODE, Systems Engineering students from Universidad Santo Tomás, Tunja (Colombia). We're into software development, cybersecurity and data analysis, working with good practices and agile methods. We want to use NASA data to monitor wildfires, a key issue in Colombia.
summary:
Fire seems to "explode" in 2012 in NASA's satellite record. It didn't: the sensor changed. MODIS (1 km, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) count fires differently, so their numbers cannot be compared directly, and any trend or alert built on mixed counts is wrong from the start.

Ember fixes that for every country on Earth. From NASA FIRMS active-fire detections we keep vegetation fires, measure the VIIRS/MODIS ratio on the months both sensors overlap, and merge MODIS with rescaled VIIRS by inverse variance, with a 90% uncertainty interval. The result is one harmonized record in MODIS-equivalent detections, so 2005 and 2023 are finally on the same scale.

On that record, Ember watches for the unusual: each month is compared with the same season across 26 years, and when fire breaks the norm it raises an alert and names the authority to notify, in 234 countries.

We are a Colombian team, so we went deepest at home: every detection since 2000, alerts for each of Colombia's departments, and the national and regional authorities that respond. Colombia is our proof that a global record can become local action; the same method is ready for any country.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ember is a web application that answers two questions for any place on Earth: when does it burn, and when is it unusual? It harmonizes the MODIS and VIIRS active-fire records into one continuous series from 2000 to today and turns that series into early-warning alerts.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: NASA FIRMS standard products for MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra/Aqua) and VIIRS 375 m (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), plus FIRMS near-real-time data for recent days.

2. Filtering: only vegetation fires; volcanoes, gas flares, industrial sources and low-confidence detections are removed.

3. Aggregation: daily and monthly detection counts and mean fire radiative power (FRP, MW) per country and subdivision.

4. Cross-calibration: the VIIRS/MODIS ratio k is measured on the months where both sensors exist (from February 2012), with shrinkage toward a prior when overlap is short.

5. Harmonization: MODIS and VIIRS/k are merged by inverse variance, H = (w_M M + w_V V/k) / (w_M + w_V), with a 90% interval. Values are MODIS-equivalent detections, so any two years are directly comparable. Before 2012 only MODIS existed and the record says so.

6. Anomalies: each period is compared with the same time of year across the whole record (seasonal z-score in standard deviations on log activity, plus a robust MAD-based score), so a busy month in the normal dry season is not flagged just for being busy.

7. Alerts: a global early-warning monitor ranks countries and Colombian departments, shows the competent civil-protection or environmental authority, issues CAP-1.2-style plain-language bulletins with recommended actions, and offers email subscriptions.

WHAT USERS SEE

An interactive 3D globe with real satellite orbits (SGP4 from TLEs) and the day/night terminator; a burn-activity calendar (day/week/month) with the typical year and its 10th–90th percentile band; NASA GIBS satellite imagery of the selected day; an El Niño / La Niña panel (NOAA ONI), shown as context, never as a proven cause; CSV downloads of what is on screen; a methodology page with every formula, assumption and limitation; and a help assistant. English and Spanish.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Fire records are often compared across years without noticing that the sensor changed in 2012. Ember removes that trap and gives emergency managers, firefighters, officials, journalists and students one honest, comparable number, its uncertainty and who to contact when it is out of the ordinary. It works for every country on Earth.

WHY COLOMBIA

We are four students from Colombia, and we built Ember to be useful first where we live. Colombia gets the deepest level: every individual detection since 2000, alerts for each of its departments, and the authorities that actually respond (UNGRD, IDEAM and the regional autonomous corporations). A department official can see that this month is far above its own normal and know whom to call. Colombia is our proof that a global satellite record can become local action, and the same method can be taken to that depth in any other country.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js (React Three Fiber), D3, GSAP, TanStack Query, Zustand, satellite.js, Tailwind CSS. Backend: Python, FastAPI, pandas, PyArrow, Pydantic. AI wording: an LLM via the Groq API (optional; deterministic templates otherwise). Deployment: Vercel (site and Python API on one domain), GitHub Actions CI/CD (type-check, build, ruff, mypy, pytest with ≥80% coverage), custom domain nasaspace.site.

Source code: https://github.com/IngeNelsonG/NASA_CHALLENGE_2026

CREATIVITY

One WebGL Earth is shared by the intro, the hero and the explorer; hotspots are drawn in a single GPU draw call; the whole science is explained in plain language next to the formulas; and alerts point to real authorities instead of stopping at a chart.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty (missing observations are shown as hatched gaps, never as zero; uncertainty is always visible; detections are not burned area), accessibility (keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, a 2D map fallback without WebGL), performance on low-end phones, bilingual users in Latin America, and clearly labelled AI-generated text.
